title: ULA's Vulcan rocket is set to return to flight on Friday the 13th
author: Stephen Clark
summary_long: United Launch Alliance announced Wednesday it plans to return its Vulcan rocket to service on November 13, nine months after a solid rocket booster anomaly threw the company's 2026 launch schedule into oblivion. The return-to-flight mission will launch 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation, the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has booked to deploy the bulk of its network. The mission will lift off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, and ULA said the launch date is pending range approval. The launch is critical for ULA after its new flagship rocket suffered nozzle failures on its solid rocket boosters on two of its first four missions, most recently during a flight in February. id: space:united launch alliance announces midnovember return to fligh:2026-10-28T22:46:41.000Z
title: United Launch Alliance announces mid-November return to flight for Vulcan rocket
author: Will Robinson-Smith
summary_long: United Launch Alliance said its fledgling Vulcan rocket would return to flight Friday, November 13, after a nine-month grounding due problems with its solid rocket boosters. This mission, carrying 40 satellites for Amazon’s Leo internet service, will be the fifth flight of Vulcan since it debuted in 2024 and will be the first time it has been fitted with six strap-on solid rocket boosters. It was nozzle failures on the Northrop Grumman-built solid rockets that put Vulcan flights on hold earlier this year. The rocket’s second flight was marred by the disintegration of a nozzle on one of the two 63XL Graphite Epoxy Motors. Source: spaceflightnow.com. Date: 2026-10-28. id: space:artemis iii sls core stage joins boosters at kennedy:2026-10-28T18:59:44.000Z
title: Artemis III SLS Core Stage Joins Boosters at Kennedy
author: Tiffany L. Fairley
summary_long: NASA’s Artemis III SLS (Space Launch System) core stage is integrated alongside the twin solid rocket boosters on Oct. 28 inside the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Technicians lifted the 212-foot rocket stage from the facility’s High Bay 2 using a one-of-a kind lifting beam designed to place the stage onto the mobile launcher. Once testing and checkouts are complete, teams will roll the core stage and booster stack out to Launch Pad 39B to conduct a tanking test where liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen fuel will be loaded only into the core stage and launch teams will practice countdown procedures and timelines.
